question.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(3-x)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=2\,m/s$ at the origin, find the maximum velocity of the particle.
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14164351/assets/0f8f7773a5e55c81de553eccf684f9a6128dd6e76e06b9040d5953371e72184f.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(3-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=3-x.
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3-x & =0 \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=3\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,3)$ | $3$ | $(3,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $2$ |  | $4$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $1>0$ | $0$ | $-1<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=3\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=3-x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (3-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=3x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,{m/s}^{2}$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =3x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =3(0)-\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2}+C \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =3x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+2 \\ {v}^{2} & =6x-{x}^{2}+4 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}+4}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(3)=\sqrt{6(3)-(3)^{2}+4}=\sqrt{13}\,m/s.
$$
